news.2026-10-14-botswana-de-beers.title: Diamonds: Botswana is about to carry more weight in De Beers, the giant its owner wants to sell
news.2026-10-14-botswana-de-beers.summar: According to Bloomberg, Botswana is close to raising its stake in De Beers from 15% to about 25%. The deal is not signed, but it would remove a major obstacle to selling the company.
news.2026-10-14-botswana-de-beers.points: Botswana and the Global Diamond Consortium (GDC) are reportedly close to a deal that would raise the state's stake in De Beers from 15% to about 25%, according to sources cited by Bloomberg; nothing is signed yet, and the exact terms remain unclear [1][2].
The GDC, led by former De Beers chief Gareth Penny, was chosen in July as preferred bidder to buy De Beers from Anglo American, which owns about 85% [2].

The GDC also includes Namibia and Angola: the three states together would hold less than 50%, and private investors would keep control, even though Botswana's president Duma Boko had said he wanted a majority [1].
news.2026-10-14-botswana-de-beers.why.0: Diamonds keep Botswana running, so the state's share of De Beers matters far more than an ordinary investment. As long as the country had not agreed, the sale of the company stayed blocked [2].
news.2026-10-14-botswana-de-beers.why.1: If the deal is confirmed, Botswana would not get the control it asked for, but a bigger seat at the table. It would also be a rare case of three African producer countries teaming up to buy a global giant in their own resource [1].
news.2026-10-14-botswana-de-beers.forMe: Nearly all the diamond rings and jewellery you see in shop windows go through De Beers. Whoever owns the group influences the supply of diamonds, so their price, and decides how much stays in the producing countries.

news.2026-10-14-coree-puces-chute-bourse: Seoul: the stock market plunges more than 5% in one session, because of a Chinese memory chipmaker
The Kospi lost 5.5% on Tuesday. Investors fear that a Chinese rival to Samsung and SK hynix will push memory chip prices down.
The Kospi, the Seoul stock index, closed on Tuesday 13 October at 6,035.35 points, down 5.46%, after falling as much as 7.41% during the session [1][2].

The drop followed an announcement by China's CXMT, which plans to launch a new type of server DRAM memory by the end of the year; analysts see a risk of price pressure on South Korean manufacturers [1].
Foreign investors sold 4.53 trillion won (about $3.4 billion) of shares, and the index has lost nearly 14% in five sessions [1].
South Korea lives largely off its memory chips: Samsung and SK hynix weigh very heavily on the stock market. When fear of a Chinese rival appears, the whole index wobbles [1].

The United States has long tried to hold China back on chips. This session shows that Beijing is moving forward in memory anyway, and that markets take it seriously. Fading enthusiasm for AI and oil near a two-week high also played a part, according to the press [1].

Memory chips are in your phone, your computer and AI servers. If a new manufacturer pushes their prices down, your devices may get cheaper in time, but the economy of a country like South Korea suffers.

news.2026-10-14-chine-sanctions-belize-p: Beijing sanctions two Latin American ministers because their countries keep Taiwan as an ally
China targeted Paraguay's communications minister and Belize's foreign minister. Washington denounces "coercion".

On Monday 12 October, China sanctioned Gustavo Villate, Paraguay's communications minister, and Francis Fonseca, Belize's foreign minister: their assets in China are frozen, they are barred from entering Hong Kong and Macao, and Chinese people and organisations can no longer deal with them [1].
Beijing accuses some "anti-China politicians" of pushing their countries to keep diplomatic relations with Taiwan [1].
The US State Department replied that Washington opposes China's "coercion" against countries in the hemisphere; Taiwan speaks of "transnational repression" [1][2].
Paraguay and Belize are among only 12 countries that still officially recognise Taiwan [1]. Beijing is sending them a message: keeping Taiwan has a price, including for their leaders.
It is a way to apply pressure without tariffs or an army, by targeting individuals. It adds to the rivalry between Washington and Beijing for influence in Latin America.

This kind of tug-of-war decides who builds a country's ports, roads and 5G networks. The more China and the United States compete over Latin America, the more carefully European companies have to choose their partners.
countries only still have official diplomatic relations with Taiwan, including Paraguay and Belize
news.2026-10-14-ukraine-treve-energetiqu: Trump announces an "energy truce" in Ukraine, but the strikes continue
Donald Trump says an energy ceasefire is in force. Kyiv says Russia has already hit at least six energy sites since, and Europe has doubts.

On Sunday 11 October, Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" on Truth Social; Volodymyr Zelensky says Russian forces have struck at least six Ukrainian energy facilities since, and Trump acknowledges violations on both sides [1].
The Kremlin says talks are under way, but rejects Zelensky's proposal of a 60-day truce to hold elections [1][3].

The announcement came two days after a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel; German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is keeping sanctions in place, and the EU added 1,600 people and entities to its list [3]. Berlin and Kyiv judge the truce too narrow: it should also protect Ukraine's power grid [2].
Refineries and power plants have become targets: hitting them pushes fuel prices up and plunges cities into darkness. An energy truce would therefore help everyone, if it held [1].

But it also shows a disagreement between Washington, which is easing some sanctions, and Europe, which is tightening them. The two camps are not talking about the same thing: Trump mainly targets refineries, while Kyiv and Berlin also want to protect electricity [2][3].
The diesel and gas you pay for also depend on what the war does to refineries. A real truce could calm prices; a sham truce would not.

news.2026-10-14-wang-yi-bakou-balkans.ti: China's top diplomat heads to Baku and then the Balkans, as far as Montenegro
news.2026-10-14-wang-yi-bakou-balkans.su: Wang Yi attends the CICA summit in Baku, then visits Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria from 14 to 20 October. Beijing is looking for support on the road to Europe.
news.2026-10-14-wang-yi-bakou-balkans.po: China's foreign ministry announced on 12 October that Wang Yi will represent Xi Jinping at the 7th CICA summit in Baku on 15 October, on a trip running from 14 to 20 October [1][2].
He will also visit Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria; it is his first official visit to Azerbaijan in seven years [2].

According to the South China Morning Post, it would be the first visit by a Chinese foreign minister to Montenegro since the country's independence twenty years ago, a claim I could not cross-check [3]. The Chinese spokesperson cites Montenegro's North-South highway as a joint flagship project [1].
news.2026-10-14-wang-yi-bakou-balkans.wh: The CICA brings together 28 countries from Asia, including China, India, Iran, Russia and Turkey [2]. Baku, on the route between China and Europe, is a key place for Beijing.
The Balkans are at the doorstep of the European Union. Sending a minister there shows that China can fund roads and building sites where the EU hesitates, which worries some Europeans.
news.2026-10-14-wang-yi-bakou-balkans.fo: The roads, ports and railways that China finances around Europe decide which way the goods you buy online will travel tomorrow.

news.2026-10-14-gazoduc-asie-centrale-ex: An explosion hits the gas pipeline linking Central Asia to Russia, with flames 70 metres high
The "Central Asia–Center" gas pipeline exploded on Tuesday in Russia's Penza region. It was shut off; the cause is unknown and the report is not independently verified.
An explosion hit the "Central Asia–Center" gas pipeline on Tuesday 13 October near the village of Volchkovo, in the Penza region; the flames reached about 70 metres and the line was shut off [1][2].
According to first reports, there are no dead or injured; the cause is unknown and no restart date has been announced [1][2].

The network links Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan to Russia; since October 2023, part of it has been used to carry Russian gas to Uzbekistan via Kazakhstan [1]. The initial alert came from Gazprom's subsidiary Transgaz Saratov, cited by Kommersant; it is not independently verified [1][3].
This pipeline is a thread tying three Central Asian countries to Russia. If the line stays closed, the gas that flows through it has to be replaced or reduced [1].
The question of the cause remains: accident, sabotage or something else. The sources I could consult do not say, and it is best to wait for investigations before concluding [1][3].
Gas travels through long pipes that war and tensions make fragile. Every incident on these lines is a reminder that energy depends on routes no one fully controls.

news.2026-10-14-liban-mission-ue-armee.t: The European Union will train the Lebanese army as UN peacekeepers prepare to leave
news.2026-10-14-liban-mission-ue-armee.s: On Monday, EU foreign ministers created a three-year mission to advise and train Lebanon's army and security forces.
news.2026-10-14-liban-mission-ue-armee.p: On Monday 12 October, EU foreign ministers created a support mission for Lebanon, with an initial three-year mandate, both civilian and military [1][2].
The military part will advise and train the Lebanese army on border and maritime security; the civilian part will train the internal security forces, notably against cybercrime and smuggling [1][2].
According to Kaja Kallas, more than ten member states are ready to contribute; the mission does not replace the UN force, UNIFIL, whose mandate ends in December [1][2].
news.2026-10-14-liban-mission-ue-armee.w: When the peacekeepers leave, someone will have to help the Lebanese army hold the south of the country. The EU wants a place there rather than leaving a void [1].
The timetable remains vague: more planning is needed, and sources disagree on the start date. The number of troops and countries is not fixed [1][2].
news.2026-10-14-liban-mission-ue-armee.f: A Lebanon that controls its territory costs neighbouring Europe less in refugees and crises. That is the calculation behind this deployment.

news.2026-10-14-ormuz-navires-touches.ti: Hormuz: a container ship and a tanker hit by projectiles, while Washington escorts oil
news.2026-10-14-ormuz-navires-touches.su: Two ships were hit on Tuesday in the strait, with the attacker unknown. The United States says it helped move more than 19 million barrels the day before.
news.2026-10-14-ormuz-navires-touches.po: The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on Tuesday 13 October that a container ship had been hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz; another alert reported a tanker hit [1][2].
The US command CENTCOM says it helped its Gulf partners move more than 19 million barrels of crude on Monday 12 October, and rejects the Iranian Revolutionary Guards' claim to control the strait [3].

According to Iran, the US response to its proposal to reopen the strait is "insufficient"; Washington wants to discuss the nuclear programme from the start, while Tehran wants to reopen Hormuz first [4].
news.2026-10-14-ormuz-navires-touches.wh: The Strait of Hormuz is the exit door for Gulf oil. As long as ships are hit there, insurers and shipowners hesitate, and energy prices stay tense.
The 19-million-barrel figure comes from the US military itself and is not independently verified [3]. The source of the fire on the ships is not identified in the sources consulted [1][2].
news.2026-10-14-ormuz-navires-touches.fo: When oil struggles to leave the Gulf, you see it at the pump and in electricity prices in Europe, as in recent months.
